title: Peking University - Report on Overseas Clinical Clerkship
paragraphs: From March to the end of April I was allowed to go to Peking University. I did the clinical clerkship for eight weeks at Peking University People's Hospital (the Second Hospital), one of the ten affiliated hospitals of the university, spending four weeks in cardiac surgery and four weeks in cardiology.

In cardiac surgery I mainly followed the supervising teacher Dr. Han, and when he was away on outside duty, the attending Dr. Zhang. The specific content was as follows. On Mondays I attended the conference, checked the week's schedule and discussed upcoming surgical cases. From Tuesday to Friday I took part in the morning handover and ward rounds, and then observed or assisted in surgery. Between operations I learned postoperative management in the CCU. Conversations at conferences and ward rounds were mainly in Chinese, but Dr. Han and several other doctors interpreted as needed, so I could understand. The number of operations was about twice that of a university hospital, and there were many cases complicated by cardiovascular disease or malignant tumors, which was a fresh experience. Dr. Han specialises in minimally invasive surgery, and I was able to deepen my insight into cardiac surgery for cancer patients. In particular, I was surprised at the treatment plans, whose main purpose was early chemotherapy after intervention on the heart, such as surgery for a chronic myeloid leukemia patient who had received a transfusion the day before to improve anemia and surgery for a right lung cancer patient. I have heard that in Japan, cancer patients are judged to be at relatively high risk, and catheter treatment is more easily chosen than open-heart surgery. At first I only observed surgery for about a week, but afterward I was allowed to take part in the sterile field and experienced various surgical techniques. I was able to try everything from preoperative disinfection to dermal suturing, subcutaneous suturing and great saphenous vein graft harvesting. At first my technique was clumsy, but through being taught by the fellow Dr. Gau during lunch breaks and borrowing practice tools such as needle holders and forceps from Dr. Zhang, I improved as I practised repeatedly. In addition, during the cardiology period too I was permitted to observe and take part in surgery in my break time. In other words, for about two months I could observe or take part in surgery almost every day, which led to great growth in my technical skills. I felt very grateful that this practical and intensive training exceeded my expectations before the clerkship began.

In cardiology I learned under the attending Dr. Hou. I took part in morning conferences and ward rounds, took part in catheter treatment and procedures when applicable, and when not, discussed patients' conditions and treatment plans while looking at the electronic chart. The electronic chart was all in Chinese, but because it was written in Chinese characters I could understand it apart from drug names. Dr. Hou, who has experience of studying in the UK, taught me in fluent English, imitating the methods used to teach him during that time. For example, in ward rounds, after explaining each patient's case in English at the bedside, I was asked for my opinion on the treatment plan and tests, so I could learn actively. He also recommended related papers (NEJM and others), and after I read them he answered my questions and also gave a lecture on analytical methods. In the outpatient clinic I also learned about China's insurance system, prescription rules and epidemiology. In the cath lab, where several times as many cases as at Nagoya University Hospital were performed (more than 40 a day), I was impressed by the number of cases and the efficiency of the medical team. I also had the opportunity to meet Prof. Liu, who had done research on imaging tests (OCT and IVUS) in the US, and obtained advanced knowledge. After each catheter treatment, I evaluated the coronary angiography results with Dr. Hou and discussed the degree of stenosis in each segment, and through one-on-one guidance I was able to greatly improve my assessment of the degree of stenosis. I also observed emergency catheter treatment. At our university hospital I had never had the experience of observing primary PCI (emergency PCI), so it was very impressive. I was surprised that the patient's condition before PCI (chest pain and so on) changed dramatically within 15 minutes after PCI. Moreover, on the last day of the program I had a chance to give a presentation on heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. I had encountered a patient with this disease during this period, and this disease is an important risk factor not only in PCI but also in cardiac surgery. The cardiology clerkship also was wonderful, with a good balance of input and output.

Outside the clerkship, three volunteer students including Mr. Shi supported me. Especially in the first week, communication with non-hospital staff was necessary for things such as face recognition registration and dormitory payment, and their help was very useful for me, who cannot speak Chinese. After that too, we went sightseeing and ate together, talked about student life and future dreams, and deepened our bonds. Also, at the daily lunch with Dr. Hou, I learned about Chinese culture such as the Chinese poems of Du Fu and Li Bai, the costumes and lifestyles of ethnic minorities and local cuisine, and came to feel closer to China. Although the pronunciation differs, I discovered many cultural commonalities between Japan and China, and my sense of closeness to China deepened. I am also very grateful to Prof. Xu, who gave diverse support from after the destination was decided and throughout the study abroad period, such as visa applications, notifications to the public security bureau and the selection of the supervising teacher.

Finally, I sincerely thank the professors of the International Collaboration Office of Nagoya University who gave me this best of chances and supported me. I will treasure this valuable experience and the connections I made. I hope this program will continue and prosper even more.
